title: Bunions: reducing pressure, choosing treatment and planning recovery
intro: A bunion is a change in alignment around the big-toe joint, often with a bony prominence on the inner side of the foot. The big toe may lean towards the others, causing crowding, rubbing or pain. It is more than a patch of hard skin, and its appearance does not determine how much treatment is needed. Care aims to improve comfort and function; surgery is considered according to symptoms and circumstances rather than appearance alone.

sections.heading: Describe where pain and pressure occur
paragraphs: Tell the clinician whether pain is over the bump, underneath the forefoot or in crowded neighbouring toes. Explain walking distance, shoe problems, skin rubbing and restrictions at work or sport. Foot structure, family tendency and other conditions can contribute; tight shoes can aggravate pressure but are not the only explanation. A suddenly hot, very painful big-toe joint could be another problem such as gout or infection. Do not assume every new foot pain is simply the known bunion.

sections.heading: Use examination to understand the whole foot
paragraphs: Assessment considers toe alignment, joint movement, skin, circulation and the way you stand and walk. Weight-bearing X-rays may be useful when planning surgery or clarifying the deformity, but treatment is not chosen from an angle alone. Mention diabetes, poor circulation, numbness, inflammatory arthritis and previous operations. These can change what is safe and how wounds might heal. Ask whether arthritis or another source of pain is present as well, and what a podiatry or specialist review would add.

sections.heading: Try practical pressure relief with realistic expectations
paragraphs: Shoes with enough width and depth around the toes can reduce rubbing; check the fit while standing rather than buying a larger size that slips elsewhere. Suitable padding, insoles or toe spacers may help selected symptoms, but must not create new pressure. Ask for fitting advice, particularly with reduced sensation or fragile skin. These measures can improve comfort but do not reliably straighten an established deformity. Be cautious about products promising permanent correction. A pharmacist or clinician can advise suitable pain relief alongside your other medicines and conditions.

sections.heading: Compare surgery with continued symptom management
paragraphs: Surgery may be discussed when pain and functional limitation remain troublesome despite appropriate measures. Procedures vary and may realign bones and soft tissues rather than merely shaving off a bump. Ask which operation is proposed, why it suits your foot and what it can realistically improve. Risks include infection, stiffness, nerve symptoms, persistent pain, recurrence and problems with bone healing. Footwear choices may still be limited afterwards. An operation is not automatically necessary because a bunion is visible, and the recovery demands should be part of the decision.

sections.heading: Plan everyday help and protect skin during follow-up
paragraphs: After surgery, instructions about weight-bearing, special footwear, elevation, dressings, driving and work depend on the procedure. Arrange help and transport before treatment and do not copy another patient's timetable. Persistent swelling can outlast the initial wound healing, so ask what changes are expected. Increasing wound pain, spreading redness, discharge or fever needs prompt advice; a cold, pale or suddenly numb foot requires urgent assessment. New calf swelling or breathlessness also needs urgent help, with emergency care for chest pain or severe breathing difficulty. Without surgery, review worsening pain, skin breakdown or reduced mobility rather than enduring them indefinitely.

examples.title: Hypothetical example: checking footwear and padding
examples.text: A person has rubbing over a bunion during long shifts. They try appropriately wide shoes and ask a podiatrist about padding. They check for new pressure marks rather than expecting a spacer to permanently move the bones back into place.

examples.title: Hypothetical example: deciding about surgery
examples.text: Someone with persistent walking pain asks about the proposed correction, its risks and time away from standing work. They discuss home help and alternatives before booking, rather than choosing surgery solely to fit a narrow style of shoe.

questions: Is the bunion the main source of my pain, and do circulation, nerves or arthritis change the plan?
Which shoes, supports or pain-relief options are suitable, and what can they realistically achieve?
If considering surgery, what benefits, risks and recovery support apply to my procedure?
